Anika Wells says welfare checks related to Triple Zero calls are "ongoing". (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

Telstra officials notified the office of Communications Minister Anika Wells about a widespread mobile and data outage hours after initial problems were detected.

The network crash has sparked a political stoush over a senior Liberal test-calling Triple Zero, as well as unfounded suggestions of foreign interference.

Telstra says the outage has been resolved, but has flagged a "secondary issue" potentially including Triple Zero calls.

Telstra informed the office of Communications Minister Anika Wells about a widespread mobile outage potentially impacting millions of Australians about two and a half hours after first detecting an issue.

State and territory police have been conducting welfare checks on dozens of individuals who had calls to Triple Zero (000) drop out during the network crash on Wednesday, which also stalled regional train services and affected payment processing for businesses.

A senior Liberal has also denied breaking the law by test-calling the emergency number to ascertain if there were connection issues, a move criticised by Labor as "outrageous".

Telstra reported at around 4pm on Wednesday that the outage had been resolved, but by the evening flagged a "secondary issue" related to some calls, including those to Triple Zero.

It said where there was an issue connecting to the emergency service line, the caller may be connected to an alternative network and, if a failed Triple Zero call was detected, a welfare check would be ordered.

Telstra says its services have been mostly restored after a nationwide outage that impacted potentially millions of Australians.

The telco first identified a problem impacting "some" mobile phone calls and data services at about 4.30am on Wednesday, with Telstra advising Ms Wells's staff about the network crash at about 7am.

The information was immediately passed on to the minister, who returned from leave to respond to the situation and declared it was on Telstra to explain to Australians how and why it had happened.

Telstra briefly put a message about the outage on its website at about 6:15am and provided comment to media at about 6:35am — before Ms Wells's office was directly informed.

Telstra has defended its communication process, insisting the government and other stakeholders were informed "very, very early" in the morning.

Ms Wells said a "detailed" timeline of the incident was being collated by Australia's Triple Zero custodian, noting this was one of the lessons from last year's Optus outage.

Ms Wells said telcos were already the least-trusted industry in the country and that it would be up to Telstra to "make things right".

She also confirmed the government had been advised that some callers had been unable to connect to Triple Zero and as at 10.25am about "three dozen" welfare checks were ongoing.

"The Triple Zero custodian is in regular communication with Telstra to receive updates on the progress and outcomes of these checks," she said.

In an update shortly after 5pm, Telstra confirmed 333 welfare checks had been conducted, with the company unable to reach 79 individuals. They were then referred to state authorities.

Telstra confirmed 333 welfare checks had been conducted. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Victoria Police was asked to conduct 32 checks, while NSW were following up 13 callers, of which four remained "outstanding" as of 4:30pm.

Tasmania completed three checks, South Australia had no checks to make and Western Australia conducted one that turned out to be a person who had not meant to call Triple Zero.

Ms Wells said Australians were rightly "horrified" by the Optus outage in September last year where calls failed to connect to Triple Zero, but insisted the Telstra incident was a "very different kind of outage".

She said the government had been advised so-called "camp-on" arrangements, in which a phone automatically jumps onto another available network to make emergency calls, had been "working" during the Telstra incident.

Ms Wells suggested some of the dropped calls might relate to instances where the person got through to Triple Zero on a second attempt.

Coalition Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson has defended her decision to conduct test-calls of the Triple Zero line on Wednesday morning, rejecting suggestions she had broken the law.

Deliberately making non-emergency, nuisance or hoax calls is an offence under Commonwealth law, and can carry a maximum sentence of up to three years in jail.

Senator Henderson confirmed she had called Triple Zero on Wednesday morning out of concern about a potential outage and failed to connect to the service twice.

She then informed her experience "directly to Telstra".

Sarah Henderson has defended making two test Triple Zero calls. (ABC News: Sarah Henderson)

Senator Henderson said she had not broken the law, as it related to "vexatious or hoax calls".

"I was clearly concerned about the wellbeing and safety of Australians," she said.

"The bottom line is I'm doing my job and I don't have trust in this government and I have very low trust in our telecommunications carriers after what we saw last year [with the Optus outage]."

Acting Transport Minister Kristy McBain was critical of Senator Henderson's actions.

"We teach our kids not to prank call Triple Zero, and I think it is absolutely outrageous that the shadow communications minister has been making test calls to Triple Zero at a time where we need to make sure that we are doing as many welfare checks as possible and making sure that that network is open to people in emergency situations," she said.

Telstra chief financial officer Michael Ackland said he believed the government was informed about the outage "very, very early" on Wednesday.

"It may have been a couple of hours after 4:30 in the morning as teams were working through various issues," he said.

"But we worked very hard to keep government and other stakeholders informed as absolutely as quickly as we could and from very, very early this morning."

Mr Ackland said the crash was caused by malfunctioning "nodes", but the root cause of that issue was not yet known.

Michael Ackland said he believed Telstra informed the government about the outage “very, very early” (ABC News)

Mobile phones and data services linked to Telstra experienced intermittent outages, with the company reporting about 90 per cent of affected services returned to normal by Wednesday afternoon.

Telstra has about 11 million customers in Australia, but when asked about the extent of the outage Mr Ackland suggested "thousands" of people had been affected before conceding it could be "hundreds of thousands".

Chief executive Vicki Brady is overseas, but Mr Ackland confirmed that she was returning from leave early and would be back in the country by Friday morning.

A Telstra spokesperson said Mr Ackland was "managing the issue" and that Ms Brady had been "briefed and kept updated throughout".

The government has also criticised members of the Coalition and crossbench for implying the outage could be linked to the Chinese missile test in the Pacific on Monday.

Ms Wells accused One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor of "going off half-cocked" about the possibility of foreign interference without any evidence.

"What I can confirm, as the comms minister, is that Telstra says there is no evidence to suggest that is the case," Ms Wells said.

"I think those parliamentarians should account for why they would behave so irresponsibly on a day when people just want their services back online."

A resident in a bushfire zone says they were left in a "blind panic" after their mobile phone couldn't connect, as an advocate warns of more system failures if major changes aren't made.

Ms Wells said she had spoken to Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke about the potential of foul play and was "assured by his answers" there was nothing to suggest it at this time.

"I'm sure that as we get more information, we would be happy to provide that to you, but as of today, there is no current evidence to suggest that is the case, apart from two parliamentarians going off half-cocked, to be honest," she said.

Earlier Mr Taylor had said he could "understand" Australians questioning the timing of the Telstra incident and China's missile test.

"I don't know whether there's any connection or not," he said.

Mr Joyce had called for a "diligent process" to determine if the Telstra outage was linked to foreign interference involving China.

"I don't want to be paranoid or a conspiracy theorist, but we know there is the capacity for China to affect that sort of software and that sort of network," he told Sky News.
